case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Double Jeopardy Clause (and related statutory-construction principles) allow a court to impose cumulative sentences for a single act of using a firearm during a Hobbs Act robbery that results in death, by convicting and sentencing under both 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Double Jeopardy Clause); 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(j).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Barrett argues that § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both are based on the same conduct and predicate crime (here, the same Hobbs Act robbery), so there is a presumption Congress did not authorize two punishments for the same offense; because Congress did not clearly indicate an intent to permit cumulative punishments between § 924(c) and § 924(j)—unlike other contexts where Congress expressly authorizes cumulation—the Double Jeopardy Clause (or at least the rule of lenity / clear-statement principles tied to it) bars imposing both sentences for the same act.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Although the United States ultimately supports petitioner on the merits in the merits briefing excerpted here, the judgment-below position (advanced by the court-appointed amicus defending the Second Circuit) is that cumulative punishments are permitted because Congress structured § 924(j) as an offense that incorporates a § 924(c) violation and then adds the death-resulting element, and Congress’s intent to allow additional punishment for firearm use in connection with violent crimes can be sufficiently clear even if § 924(j) itself lacks separate consecutive-sentencing language; relying on cases like Missouri v. Hunter, the argument is that only one statute needs to clearly authorize additional punishment and § 924(c) already establishes an additive punishment scheme.
key_precedents: Flowers v. Mississippi, 136 S. Ct. 2157 (2016) (Alito, J., dissenting) (GVR discussion)
Garland v. Range, No. 23-374 (brief cited for holding practice)
Delligatti v. United States, No. 23-825 (pending, referenced)

John Roberts.reasoning: The government’s strongest point is that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language reflects a general anti-merger policy, but that text is most naturally read—as Justice Kavanaugh notes—to require cumulation with the predicate crime of violence or drug-trafficking crime, not with an aggravated offense (§ 924(j)) that already makes “a violation of subsection (c)” an element and provides its own penalty. Under Blockburger, when both counts rest on the same firearm use and the same predicate, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j); Whalen and Missouri v. Hunter (as Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett emphasize) require a clear statement before we authorize cumulative punishment for greater/lesser-included offenses, and § 924(j) contains none. No colleague has identified precedent or text that squarely rebut this clear-statement requirement, so a narrow holding—limited to same-conduct, same-predicate cases—best preserves statutory fidelity and institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best textual point is that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing commands implicitly require a separate § 924(c) sentence even when § 924(j) is charged, but that inference stretches § 924(c)’s directives beyond what they say and supplies a cumulation rule Congress omitted from § 924(j). As Chief Justice Roberts explains, § 924(j) incorporates “a violation of subsection (c)” as an element and then provides its own penalties, so on these facts § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense under Blockburger; Whalen and Missouri v. Hunter require a clear statement before allowing cumulative punishment for a greater and its lesser-included offense. Justice Kavanaugh’s point reinforces that § 924(c)’s additive language naturally targets stacking with the predicate offense, not with an aggravated variant that already subsumes the § 924(c) violation. Under a textualist/originalist approach, statutory silence in § 924(j) cannot do the work the government demands, so my vote remains for petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best textual hook remains § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language, but I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that this language is naturally aimed at cumulating the § 924(c) punishment with the predicate crime of violence/drug trafficking—not with an aggravated offense like § 924(j) that already makes “a violation of subsection (c)” an element and supplies its own penalty scheme. Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Whalen usefully sharpens the point: absent a clear statement, we do not infer cumulative punishment for greater/lesser-included offenses from general statutory signals, and Missouri v. Hunter demands that clarity when Congress intends stacking. On a practical level, reading § 924(c) to require automatic add-on sentences whenever prosecutors also charge § 924(j) would create severe, duplicative mandatory exposure without the kind of unmistakable congressional directive the multiple-punishments cases require. Nothing raised in conference supplies the necessary clear authorization to rebut the Blockburger presumption on these facts.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing directives should carry over to require an extra § 924(c) sentence whenever § 924(j) is charged, but that is exactly the sort of inference Whalen and Missouri v. Hunter reject absent a clear statement authorizing cumulative punishment for greater/lesser-included offenses. Chief Justice Roberts persuasively grounds the textual distinction: § 924(c)’s additive language is naturally aimed at stacking with the predicate crime, while § 924(j) incorporates the § 924(c) violation as an element yet supplies its own penalty provision without any express “plus § 924(c)” command. Justice Kagan’s practical concern reinforces my approach: reading silent overlap to mandate automatic double punishment would predictably expand prosecutorial leverage and mandatory exposure for the same firearm use, with especially harsh real-world effects on vulnerable defendants, without unmistakable congressional direction. On these facts, Blockburger’s lesser-included-offense presumption controls and is not rebutted, and lenity/avoidance principles confirm that only one punishment is authorized.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s best shot is to treat § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)’s consecutive-sentencing command (and the broader “in addition to” language) as a clear authorization to stack a § 924(c) sentence on top of a § 924(j) sentence whenever the same conduct is charged. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, that text is naturally aimed at cumulating § 924(c) with the predicate crime, not silently mandating an extra § 924(c) term when Congress separately created § 924(j) as an aggravated offense that already incorporates a § 924(c) violation and supplies its own penalties. Under Whalen and Missouri v. Hunter (as Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Barrett emphasize), when one count is a greater offense that includes the other on these facts, we require a clear statement for cumulative punishments—and § 924(j) contains none. I therefore remain with petitioner because the most coherent, workable reading is that § 924(j) is an aggravated alternative for the same firearm use, not an automatic § 924(c)-plus add-on absent explicit statutory language.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best contention is that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing commands must carry over because § 924(j) occurs “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” but that treats a directive written for § 924(c) as an unexpressed instruction to impose two punishments for the same incorporated § 924(c) violation. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh persuasively frame it, on these facts § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) under Blockburger, so Whalen’s presumption against cumulative punishment applies and Missouri v. Hunter requires a clear statement to rebut it. Section 924(j) supplies its own penalty provision yet says nothing about an additional, consecutive § 924(c) sentence—especially notable because Congress knew exactly how to demand consecutiveness and cumulation when it wished to do so in § 924(c) itself. Under a textualist approach, that silence cannot be converted into extra mandatory punishment, and lenity/separation-of-powers principles confirm the same result.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing directives implicitly require an extra § 924(c) sentence even when the same conduct is charged under § 924(j). But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, that additive/consecutive language is naturally aimed at cumulating § 924(c) with the predicate crime, not at silently mandating cumulative punishment for a greater offense (§ 924(j)) that expressly requires proof of “a violation of subsection (c)” and contains its own penalty provision. Under Blockburger and Whalen, the incorporated § 924(c)(1)(A) offense is a lesser-included offense on these facts, and Missouri v. Hunter demands a clear congressional statement to authorize cumulative punishments for greater/lesser-included offenses—something § 924(j) does not provide. Justice Barrett’s point reinforces that we should not treat § 924(c)’s general consecutive rule as a hidden stacking command in § 924(j), especially given the practical sentencing consequences and the Court’s institutional interest in clear, workable rules in criminal punishment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest textual move is that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing commands should automatically carry over when § 924(j) is charged, effectively making § 924(j) a § 924(c)-plus regime. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, that consecutive/additive language is naturally read to require cumulation with the predicate “crime of violence or drug trafficking crime,” not to silently authorize a second punishment for the very same incorporated § 924(c) violation that is an element of § 924(j). Under Blockburger, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) on these facts, and Whalen/Missouri v. Hunter require a clear statement to permit multiple punishments for greater/lesser-included offenses—something § 924(j) conspicuously lacks despite providing its own penalty provision. I therefore see no basis, consistent with textualism and the rule-of-construction function of Blockburger in the multiple-punishments setting, to infer stacking from statutory silence; lenity reinforces that conclusion.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing directives suggest Congress wanted stacking broadly, even when death results. But as Chief Justice Roberts explains, that language is naturally aimed at cumulating § 924(c) with the predicate offense, and it does not supply the kind of unmistakable authorization Missouri v. Hunter requires to impose two punishments where, under Blockburger, § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) on these facts. Justice Kagan’s emphasis on Whalen reinforces my view that we should not treat statutory silence in § 924(j) as a license for duplicative mandatory punishment, especially given the practical consequences for charging leverage and sentencing severity. Absent a clear statement in § 924(j) directing an additional, consecutive § 924(c) sentence for the same incorporated conduct, lenity and fairness principles counsel against cumulation.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Blockburger, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both rest on the same firearm use and the same predicate Hobbs Act robbery, because § 924(j) incorporates a § 924(c) violation and adds the death-resulting element. In the multiple-punishments context, the Double Jeopardy Clause turns on legislative authorization, and Missouri v. Hunter permits cumulation only where Congress has clearly indicated that intent. Here, Congress expressly made § 924(c) punishment “in addition to” the predicate crime of violence or drug-trafficking crime, but provided no comparably clear statement authorizing cumulative punishment between § 924(c) and § 924(j) for the same conduct. Respecting that textual choice and applying the presumption against cumulation for greater/lesser-included offenses, I would hold that imposing both sentences exceeds Congress’s authorization.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause permits cumulative punishments only when Congress clearly authorizes them, and absent such clarity we apply the Blockburger lesser-included-offense presumption as a rule of statutory construction. Section 924(j) expressly incorporates a "violation of subsection (c)" and then adds the death-resulting element, so when both counts rest on the same firearm use during the same Hobbs Act robbery, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) under Blockburger v. United States. Unlike § 924(c), § 924(j) contains no textual command requiring an additional consecutive punishment on top of a § 924(c) sentence, so the statutes’ text does not clearly authorize two punishments for the same offense and we should not infer such authorization. Under Missouri v. Hunter, cumulative sentences are allowed only when the legislature’s intent is clear; here, the better reading is that Congress provided alternative penalty provisions (with § 924(j) as the aggravated form) rather than an automatic stack of both.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 924(j) expressly requires proof of “a violation of subsection (c),” making § 924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense under Blockburger v. United States, 284 U.S. 299 (1932), when both counts rest on the same firearm use in the same Hobbs Act robbery. Under Missouri v. Hunter, 459 U.S. 359, 366 (1983), cumulative punishments in a single proceeding are permitted only if Congress clearly authorized them; otherwise the Double Jeopardy Clause prevents the court from imposing greater punishment than Congress intended. Here, while § 924(c)(1)(A) plainly mandates punishment “in addition to” the predicate offense, § 924(j) contains no comparable clear statement authorizing an additional, cumulative sentence on top of the incorporated § 924(c) offense for the same conduct. Given that textual structure and the absence of an unambiguous cumulation directive for § 924(j), the Blockburger presumption against multiple punishments is not rebutted.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: When the same firearm use during the same Hobbs Act robbery underlies both counts, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) because § 924(j) expressly incorporates a § 924(c) violation and adds only the death-resulting element, triggering the Blockburger lesser-included-offense presumption against multiple punishments for the same offense absent a clear congressional statement. Missouri v. Hunter permits cumulative punishments only when Congress has clearly authorized them, but § 924(j) lacks the kind of explicit "in addition to" or consecutive-sentencing language Congress routinely uses—including in § 924(c) itself—to unmistakably authorize stacking these two provisions for the same conduct. Given that ambiguity in a criminal sentencing scheme implicating the Double Jeopardy multiple-punishments principle, the rule of lenity/canon of constitutional avoidance favors reading the statutes to prohibit cumulative sentences here. That construction also avoids gratuitously increasing punishment in a way that can distort charging leverage and exacerbate unfairness without a clear directive from Congress.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 924(j) is best read as creating an aggravated offense that incorporates a § 924(c) violation and adds the death-resulting element, making § 924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense when both counts rest on the same firearm use during the same Hobbs Act robbery. Under Blockburger, that overlap triggers a presumption against cumulative punishments, and Missouri v. Hunter allows multiple punishments only when Congress clearly authorizes them—which is not shown here by § 924(c)’s general consecutive-sentencing mandate, because § 924(j) supplies its own distinct penalty scheme without expressly requiring an additional § 924(c) sentence on top. Given the statutory structure and the absence of a clear textual signal that Congress meant to stack § 924(c) and § 924(j) for the same act, the tie goes to the defendant under traditional statutory-construction principles (including lenity) rather than reading in cumulative punishment. This construction is also more workable and coherent: it avoids turning § 924(j) into an automatic “§ 924(c)-plus” add-on that doubles punishment whenever death occurs, without Congress having said so.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 924(j) expressly requires proof of “a violation of subsection (c),” making § 924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense when both counts rest on the same firearm use and the same Hobbs Act robbery predicate. Under Blockburger v. United States, the offenses therefore do not each require proof of a fact the other does not, triggering the presumption against cumulative punishments absent a clear indication of contrary congressional intent. Missouri v. Hunter allows cumulative sentences only when Congress has clearly authorized them, and nothing in § 924(j)’s text contains the kind of clear authorization (including any consecutive-sentencing command) that would overcome the lesser-included-offense presumption. In the face of that statutory silence and the serious double-jeopardy concern, the rule of lenity and our separation-of-powers duty to leave punishment-setting to Congress reinforce the conclusion that only one punishment may be imposed for the single § 924(c) violation incorporated into § 924(j).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 924(j) expressly requires proof of “a violation of subsection (c),” making § 924(c)(1)(A) a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) under Blockburger v. United States, and thus cumulative punishments are presumptively barred absent a clear statement from Congress. Missouri v. Hunter permits cumulative sentences only when Congress clearly authorizes them, but nothing in the text of § 924(j) clearly indicates an intent to stack an additional § 924(c) punishment on top of the § 924(j) penalty for the same firearm use and the same predicate Hobbs Act robbery. Consistent with Whalen v. United States, where the Court declined to infer cumulation from less-than-clear statutory signals, judicial restraint and rule-of-lenity/clear-statement principles counsel against reading § 924(c)’s general additive scheme to silently authorize double punishment when § 924(j) already incorporates § 924(c). A contrary reading would create an unworkable and legitimacy-costly regime in which overlapping offense drafting, rather than clear legislative direction, drives extra punishment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 924(j) makes it a crime to cause death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so when both counts rest on the same firearm use and the same Hobbs Act predicate, a § 924(c)(1)(A) violation is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j). Under Blockburger as a rule of construction and this Court’s multiple-punishments cases, that overlap creates a presumption against cumulative punishments absent a clear indication Congress authorized two sentences for the same offense, see Whalen v. United States and Garrett v. United States. Unlike the Missouri statutes in Missouri v. Hunter—where the legislature “expressed its clear intent” to cumulate—§ 924(j) contains no express consecutive-sentencing or cumulation directive, and § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing language naturally fits when § 924(c) is the sole firearm count rather than an incorporated element of § 924(j). Given that ambiguity on Congress’s authorization to stack penalties for the same conduct, the Double Jeopardy–informed clear-statement/lenity principles counsel against imposing both sentences.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Because § 924(j) expressly requires proof of “a violation of subsection (c),” 18 U.S.C. § 924(j), a § 924(c)(1)(A) offense is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both convictions rest on the same firearm use during the same Hobbs Act robbery. Under Whalen v. United States, 445 U.S. 684, 691-92 (1980), cumulative punishments are presumptively barred in that circumstance absent a clear indication Congress authorized two punishments, and I do not see such a clear statement in § 924(j)’s text or structure. Missouri v. Hunter, 459 U.S. 359, 366-69 (1983), allows cumulation only when legislative authorization is clear, but importing § 924(c)’s general additive scheme is not enough to overcome the lesser-included-offense presumption here, especially given the serious practical consequences of duplicative mandatory penalties. In light of the Double Jeopardy Clause’s role in preventing courts from imposing greater punishment than Congress intended, the rule-of-lenity/clear-statement principles counsel against cumulative sentencing on these facts.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Double Jeopardy Clause allows a defendant to receive cumulative punishments for the same conduct under both 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(j).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. V (Double Jeopardy Clause); 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) and 18 U.S.C. § 924(j).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Barrett argues that § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both counts arise from the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, so there is a presumption Congress did not authorize multiple punishments for the same act; because Congress did not clearly express an intent to permit stacking § 924(c) and § 924(j) sentences for the same conduct, imposing cumulative sentences violates double jeopardy principles (or, at minimum, the statutory-construction rules that avoid double-jeopardy concerns).
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States (in its merits briefing) supports petitioner: it contends that because § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), cumulative punishments are presumptively unauthorized absent a clear contrary statement from Congress; Congress elsewhere expressly authorizes certain cumulative punishments within § 924(c) but did not do so for the § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing, so the presumption against cumulative punishment is not rebutted and Barrett may not be sentenced on both counts for the same conduct (while court-appointed amicus defends the judgment below, relying on structural/history arguments and cases like Missouri v. Hunter to argue Congress intended cumulative punishment even if only one statute contains explicit “in addition to” language).

Garland v. Range, No. 23-374 (U.S. filing referenced for 'hold' practice)
Delligatti v. United States, No. 23-825 (pending, referenced)

John Roberts.reasoning: Respondent’s best point—that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing commands reflect a broad anti-merger policy—still does not supply the clear statement Missouri v. Hunter requires for this specific § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing. As Justice Kavanaugh persuasively frames it, Whalen and Rutledge treat Blockburger as a presumption about congressional intent, and here § 924(j) expressly incorporates a “violation of subsection (c)” as an element, making § 924(c) lesser-included when both counts rest on the same firearm use and predicate offense. Justice Thomas’s textual emphasis reinforces that if Congress wanted cumulative punishments notwithstanding that overlap, it knew how to say so unmistakably, as it did elsewhere in § 924(c) with “in addition to” language directed at the predicate crime. I would therefore adhere to a narrow, administrable merger rule limited to same-conduct, same-predicate situations, avoiding broader pronouncements about § 924(j) in other charging configurations.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest contention—invoking §924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentence directives as a general anti-merger policy—fails because Whalen and Rutledge ask whether Congress clearly authorized cumulative punishment for this specific pairing, not whether Congress generally favored severity. As Justice Kavanaugh explains, §924(j)’s text makes a “violation of subsection (c)” an element, so §924(c) is lesser-included when both counts rest on the same firearm use and predicate offense, triggering the presumption against stacking absent an unmistakable statement. The Chief Justice’s point that Congress wrote explicit “in addition to” language elsewhere in §924(c) underscores that its silence about cumulating §924(c) with §924(j) cannot be treated as clear authorization under Missouri v. Hunter. Nothing in the statutory text overcomes that presumption, so I adhere to the petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point remains that § 924(j) is a distinct homicide offense and that § 924(c)’s broader anti-merger policy implies stacking, but that inference cannot overcome Whalen/Rutledge’s presumption when one offense is wholly included in the other. As Justice Kavanaugh notes, Rutledge rejects the idea that separate codification or severe penalties alone supplies the “clear statement” Missouri v. Hunter requires; here, § 924(j)’s text (“in the course of a violation of subsection (c)”) makes a § 924(c) violation an element, so § 924(c) is lesser-included for the same gun use and predicate crime. The Chief Justice’s point is decisive for me on practical textual grounds: Congress expressly used “in addition to” language to mandate cumulation with the predicate offense, but did not do so to mandate an extra consecutive § 924(c) sentence on top of § 924(j). Absent unmistakable statutory authorization for this specific pairing, we should not approve duplicative mandatory consecutive punishment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest point is that Congress built § 924(c) to be harsh and cumulative, so we should assume stacking when death results—but that is exactly the kind of inference Missouri v. Hunter and Whalen forbid absent a clear statement for the specific pairing. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch stress, § 924(j) is triggered only “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” so § 924(c) is an element and thus a lesser-included offense under Blockburger, bringing the anti-cumulation presumption into play. Chief Justice Roberts’s observation that Congress used explicit “in addition to” language elsewhere in § 924(c) underscores that Congress knows how to authorize cumulation and did not do so here. Given the real-world severity of mandatory consecutive § 924(c) terms, I won’t read silence to permit duplicative punishment that disproportionately burdens defendants without unmistakable legislative direction.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest respondent point—flagged by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh—is that § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing language reflects a broad anti-merger policy for gun crimes, suggesting Congress would want stacking here too. But under Whalen/Rutledge the question is not general punitive intent; it is whether Congress clearly authorized cumulative punishment for this specific pairing, and § 924(j)’s text does not say “in addition to § 924(c)” or otherwise direct an extra mandatory consecutive § 924(c) term when the same conduct proves both counts. As Justice Thomas emphasizes, § 924(j) makes “a violation of subsection (c)” an element, so § 924(c) is lesser-included on the same firearm use and predicate offense, triggering the presumption against cumulation absent an unmistakable statement (Missouri v. Hunter). The most coherent, workable textual reading is merger at sentencing in the same-conduct scenario, leaving prosecutors free to charge alternatively and juries to convict, but not to impose duplicative punishments without Congress speaking plainly.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best textual move is to treat § 924(c)’s “in addition to” and consecutive-sentence directives as a general anti-merger policy that carries over to § 924(j) because § 924(j) occurs “in the course of” a § 924(c) violation. But as the Chief Justice explains, that “in addition to” clause speaks to cumulation with the predicate crime, not to stacking a § 924(c) sentence on top of a § 924(j) sentence when § 924(j) itself makes a § 924(c) violation an element. Justice Kavanaugh’s invocation of Whalen and Rutledge matters: once § 924(c) is lesser-included for the same conduct, Missouri v. Hunter requires an unmistakably clear authorization for multiple punishments, and Congress’s silence in § 924(j)—especially contrasted with its clear drafting elsewhere—cannot do that work. Under a principled textualist/originalist approach and separation-of-powers concerns, we should not infer extra mandatory consecutive punishment that Congress did not clearly enact.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The strongest respondent contention—that § 924(j) is a distinct homicide offense using § 924(c) only as a jurisdictional/definitional hook—does not overcome the Blockburger/Whalen/Rutledge presumption because § 924(j) textually makes “a violation of subsection (c)” an element, rendering § 924(c) lesser-included when the same firearm use and predicate crime underlie both counts. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, § 924(c)’s “in addition to” language is explicit as to cumulation with the predicate offense, but there is no comparable clear statement authorizing an extra mandatory consecutive § 924(c) term on top of a § 924(j) sentence for the same conduct; under Missouri v. Hunter, that silence cannot do the work. Justice Thomas’s point that we should not infer stacking authority from general congressional severity is persuasive: the question is unmistakable authorization for this pairing, not policy intuition. Given institutional and administrability concerns, I remain with a narrow merger-for-sentencing rule limited to same firearm use and same predicate offense.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Respondent’s strongest contention is that § 924(j) is a distinct homicide offense and that § 924(c)(1)(A)’s general “in addition to” and consecutive-sentencing commands implicitly authorize stacking. But as Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, Whalen and Rutledge treat Blockburger as a presumption about congressional intent, and § 924(j)’s text makes a “violation of subsection (c)” an element—so when both counts rest on the same firearm use and predicate crime, § 924(c) is lesser-included and cumulative punishment requires a clear statement under Missouri v. Hunter. Chief Justice Roberts’s point is dispositive for a textualist: Congress used explicit “in addition to” language to require cumulation with the predicate offense, yet said nothing comparably clear about cumulating § 924(c) with § 924(j), so we should not infer authorization for duplicative punishment from silence. That leaves room for consecutive sentences in other configurations (different firearm uses or predicates), but not this embedded-offense scenario.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The strongest respondent argument—that § 924(j) is merely a penalty add-on and that § 924(c)’s consecutive-sentencing commands therefore must stack—fails because it asks us to infer cumulative punishment where the statute does not speak clearly. As Justice Kagan and Chief Justice Roberts emphasize, Congress used unmistakable “in addition to” language to mandate cumulation with the predicate offense, but it did not do so to authorize an extra mandatory consecutive § 924(c) sentence on top of § 924(j) for the same firearm use and predicate crime. Given § 924(j)’s text requiring proof of “a violation of subsection (c),” § 924(c) is a lesser-included offense under Blockburger, and Whalen/Rutledge supply a presumption against multiple punishments absent the clear statement Missouri v. Hunter demands. The practical sentencing consequences of mandatory consecutive terms reinforce, for me, that we should not treat congressional silence as authorization to double-count the embedded § 924(c) offense.

John Roberts.reasoning: In the multiple-punishments context, the Double Jeopardy Clause chiefly asks whether the legislature clearly authorized cumulative punishment; absent a clear statement, courts apply the presumption against stacking when one offense is a lesser-included of the other. See Missouri v. Hunter, 459 U.S. 359, 366-368 (1983). Here, when the same firearm use and predicate crime support both counts, § 924(c)(1)(A) functions as a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), and Congress did not "crystal clear[ly]" indicate that a § 924(c) sentence must be imposed in addition to a § 924(j) sentence for the same conduct—unlike § 924(c)(1)(A)’s explicit "in addition to" language as to the predicate crime of violence or drug trafficking crime. Given that silence and the need for a narrow, administrable rule that avoids unnecessary constitutional doubt, I would hold that cumulative punishments under § 924(c) and § 924(j) for the same conduct are not authorized.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Double Jeopardy Clause permits cumulative punishments only when Congress has clearly authorized them, Missouri v. Hunter, 459 U.S. 359 (1983), and the starting point is the statutes’ text. Section 924(j) punishes causing death “in the course of a violation of subsection (c),” which necessarily incorporates all elements of § 924(c)(1)(A), making § 924(c) a lesser-included offense under the Blockburger test and triggering a presumption against multiple punishments for the same conduct. Nothing in the text of § 924(j) (or § 924(c)) clearly states that a defendant may be punished under both provisions for the same firearm use in the same predicate offense, especially given Congress’s demonstrated ability to mandate cumulative/consecutive punishment expressly elsewhere in § 924(c). Absent that clear authorization, cumulative sentences for the same conduct should not be imposed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying the Blockburger presumption as a canon of statutory construction, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) when both counts rest on the same firearm use during the same predicate crime, so cumulative punishments are presumptively unauthorized absent a clear statement from Congress. Missouri v. Hunter permits cumulative punishments only when the legislature clearly indicates that result, and nothing in the text of § 924(j) clearly authorizes stacking a separate § 924(c) sentence on top of a § 924(j) sentence for the same conduct. Congress knows how to draft explicit “in addition to” cumulative-punishment language within § 924(c), yet it did not include comparable language for the § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing, reinforcing the absence of clear authorization.
